name: New Zealand
summary: A British colony from the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), a dominion from 1907 and fully independent in practice by 1947; the first country where women won the vote (1893).

knownFor.label: Treaty of Waitangi
knownFor.note: Founding agreement between Māori chiefs and the Crown.

knownFor.label: Women’s vote
knownFor.note: First self-governing country to give women the vote.

knownFor.label: All Blacks and the haka
knownFor.note: Rugby team and Māori war dance.

climate.value: Temperate maritime: mild and wet in the west, drier in the east, subtropical in the far north and cold in the Southern Alps.

resources.value: Rich grassland for sheep and cattle, forests, fish, hydroelectric power, and gold, found in rushes in Otago and the West Coast in the 1860s.

disasters.value: Earthquakes such as Napier (1931) and Christchurch (2011), which killed 185 people, the Tarawera eruption (1886), and floods.

population.value: 4,993,923 at the 2023 census; a September 2026 estimate gives 5,357,340.

urbanisation.value: Highly urban: about a third of people live in Auckland, the largest city; Wellington is the capital and Christchurch the largest South Island city.

disease.value: Measles and flu hit Māori hard in the 1800s and 1918.

migration.value: British settlers; Pacific Islanders and Asians later.

economicBase.value: Dairy was the largest export earner (17.7% of exports, NZ$14.1 billion, in the year to June 2018); tourism was 5.6% of GDP in 2016. Meat and wool are not covered in the part of the page read.

tradeRoutes.value: Refrigerated ships carried meat to Britain from 1882.

moneyAndTax.value: The New Zealand dollar replaced the pound in 1967; taxes include income tax and a goods and services tax (GST) introduced in 1986.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy (King Charles III) with a one-chamber Parliament.

keyRulers.value: Richard Seddon led the Liberal government that took office in 1891; New Zealand gave all women the vote in 1893. Michael Joseph Savage declared war on Germany in 1939. Christopher Luxon has been prime minister since 27 November 2023. The page does not mention Jacinda Ardern.

succession.value: Prime ministers lead the party or coalition with a majority in Parliament; since 1996 elections have used mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting.

institutions.value: In 1893 New Zealand was the first nation to grant all women the right to vote.

stability.value: A stable democracy with peaceful changes of government; women won the vote in 1893, and a welfare state grew from 1938.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The New Zealand Defence Force (army, navy and air force); New Zealand troops fought in both world wars, Korea and Vietnam.

majorWars.value: The page dates armed conflict between the colonial government and Māori from 1843 (the Wairau Affray); the wars, mainly in the North Island, led to large confiscations of Māori land. It gives no end year, and Gallipoli is not covered. The entry’s earlier 1845–72 dates are not on this page.

territoryChange.value: Ruled Samoa (1914–62) and the Cook Islands from 1901; Tokelau and the Ross Dependency in Antarctica remain linked to it.

alliancesRivals.value: Joined Australia and the US in the ANZUS treaty (1951); its nuclear-free law of 1987 ended US warship visits; very close ties with Australia.

inventions.value: The jet boat, developed by Bill Hamilton in the 1950s, and the first commercial bungee-jumping site, opened near Queenstown in 1988.

scienceEducation.value: Ernest Rutherford, born near Nelson, split the atom (1917); universities include Otago (1869), and free state schooling began in 1877.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Railways from the 1860s, the North Island Main Trunk line (1908), state highways, Cook Strait ferries and air links through Auckland.

languageWriting.value: English, and te reo Māori, made an official language in 1987; New Zealand Sign Language became official in 2006.

artsArchitecture.value: Māori carving and meeting houses (wharenui), writers such as Katherine Mansfield, painters such as Colin McCahon, and a large film industry.

socialStructure.value: European, Māori, Pacific and Asian New Zealanders.

sharedIdentity.value: A bicultural identity based on the Treaty of Waitangi, plus pride in sport (the All Blacks), the outdoors and the Anzac legacy.

dailyLife.value: Most people live in detached houses in towns; foods include lamb, fish and chips, hāngī and pavlova, and rugby is a national passion.

neighbours.value: Australia across the Tasman Sea, and Pacific island nations such as Fiji, Tonga, Samoa and the Cook Islands.

ideasReligions.value: Social reform: votes for women (1893), old-age pensions (1898) and a welfare state under the Social Security Act (1938).

colonisation.value: A British colony after the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), self-governing from 1852–56, and a dominion from 1907.

riseSignals.value: Polynesian settlement between about 1280 and 1350 (recent sources favour the 14th century); Abel Tasman was the first European to sight it, in 1642.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; living standards were among the world’s highest in the 1950s and 1960s, when farm exports boomed.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: The Treaty of Waitangi was first signed on 6 February 1840; a dominion in 1907; adopted the Statute of Westminster in 1947.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
